title: Projectile motion
examples: How does the initial angle affect the range?
Is the horizontal velocity constant throughout the flight?
What is the time taken to reach maximum height?

explain.say: When an object flies through the air, its motion is split into two parts. We call these parts independent horizontal and vertical motion.
For the horizontal part, we assume no air resistance acts upon the object. This means the horizontal velocity stays constant throughout the entire flight.
For the vertical part, the only force acting is gravity pulling it down. This causes a constant downward acceleration, which is the acceleration due to gravity, g.
The maximum height is reached when the object's vertical velocity momentarily becomes zero. After this point, the object starts falling back down.
The horizontal range is the total horizontal distance the object travels before it lands back at the same height. This depends on both the initial speed and the launch angle.

draw.text: Range depends on initial speed and angle

faq.q: Does the object need to land at the same height to calculate the range?
faq.a: Yes, for the standard range formula to apply easily, the landing height should match the starting height. If they are different, you must use more complex equations.
asks: What if it lands on a slope?
Does the starting and ending height matter for range?

faq.q: If I throw something straight up, what is the horizontal range?
faq.a: If you throw it straight up, it has no initial horizontal velocity. Therefore, its horizontal range will be zero. It just goes up and comes back down.
asks: What is the range when the angle is ninety degrees?
If vx is zero, what is the range?

faq.q: Is the vertical motion always slower than the horizontal motion?
faq.a: No, the vertical motion changes constantly due to gravity. The horizontal motion is constant only if we ignore air resistance. They are independent motions.
asks: Is one motion always faster than the other?

faq.q: How do I find the time of flight?
faq.a: The time of flight is the total time the object spends in the air. You find this using the vertical motion equations, often by setting the final vertical position to zero.
asks: How long is the object airborne?
What determines the total time in the air?

faq.q: Does the initial speed affect the maximum height?
faq.a: Yes, a higher initial speed will result in a greater maximum height. The vertical component of that initial speed determines how high it goes.
asks: If I throw it harder, does it go higher?

facts: Horizontal velocity remains constant if air resistance is ignored.
Vertical motion is governed by the acceleration due to gravity, g.
At the maximum height, the vertical component of velocity is zero.
The time of flight is determined entirely by the initial vertical velocity.

quiz.say: A ball is launched with an initial speed of ten meters per second at an angle of thirty degrees. What is its horizontal velocity?
quiz.why: The horizontal velocity only depends on the initial speed and the cosine of the launch angle.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it incorrectly uses the sine function instead of the cosine function.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the horizontal motion is constant and does not stop at the peak.
wrong.3: This is wrong because it ignores the effect of the launch angle on the horizontal speed.

quiz.say: If an object is thrown straight up, what is its horizontal range?
quiz.why: Since there is no initial horizontal push, the object never travels any horizontal distance.

wrong.1: This is wrong because the speed only matters if there is an angle to the throw.
wrong.2: This is wrong because gravity only affects the vertical movement, not the horizontal range.
wrong.3: This is wrong because even if it flies for a long time, it never moves sideways.

quiz.say: A projectile reaches its maximum height. At this exact point, what is its vertical velocity?
quiz.why: The object momentarily stops moving up before it begins to fall back down, making its vertical speed zero.

wrong.1: This is wrong because gravity has slowed the object down from its starting vertical speed.
wrong.2: This is wrong because acceleration is the rate of change, not the instantaneous velocity at the peak.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the vertical velocity is what is changing to zero at the peak.
